summary: Proposes new MIME media subtypes, Text/SGML and Application/SGML, for carrying SGML documents. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1874 proposes two MIME labels for SGML content. The sender chooses between them based on whether a person can understand the entity without an SGML processor.

questions: what is the text/sgml media type
how to label sgml in mime
subtitle: Two proposed MIME media types for sending SGML entities and documents.

tldr.problem: SGML entities need media type labels when exchanged through MIME. Existing registered media types did not cover the SGML entities described by the memo.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes Text/SGML for entities a person can understand without SGML processing, and Application/SGML for other entities. Optional parameters describe character encoding and SGML-specific information.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1874 is Experimental and does not specify an Internet standard. It proposes media types for exchanging SGML content.

today: RFC 1874 is Experimental and does not specify an Internet standard. The RFC metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why SGML Needs MIME Types
sections.content:
SGML encodes document structure using tags and rules. The memo says that SGML document parts need to be transferable, and that basic media types should be registered for SGML entities not covered by existing types.

RFC 1874 proposes the Text/SGML and Application/SGML media subtypes. It defines their parameters and explains which subtype to use for different content.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIME media type identifies the kind of content in a message. This RFC proposes labels for SGML entities so receiving software can choose how to handle them.

sections.title: Text/SGML and Application/SGML
sections.content:
Text/SGML is for SGML entities intended to be readable by a person without SGML display software. Each SGML record must correspond to a line in the MIME body. The media type provides a fallback to plain text for systems without SGML support.

Application/SGML is for entities that do not meet those conditions. Its record-start and record-end characters must be explicitly represented using the bit combinations specified by the SGML declaration.
sections.plainLanguage: Use Text/SGML when a person can read the content without SGML software. Use Application/SGML when the receiver must process SGML structure to understand it.

sections.title: Character and Encoding Parameters
sections.content:
Both subtypes can use SGML-bctf and SGML-boot. The SGML-bctf parameter identifies how the SGML bit combinations are transformed into the MIME body's octet stream; its default is identity, meaning no transformation.

Text/SGML also has a charset parameter, whose default is us-ascii. The SGML-boot parameter identifies another MIME part with information needed to interpret the character set of a document entity.
sections.plainLanguage: Parameters tell an SGML-aware receiver how the document's character values were turned into transmitted octets. Text/SGML can also name a character set for systems that do not process SGML.

sections.title: Processing Untrusted SGML
sections.content:
The RFC warns that an SGML entity can contain instructions for a recipient's parser or presentation system. If that software allows system commands to run during processing, an untrusted entity could cause those commands to execute.

Recipients should consider this risk when processing SGML from untrusted sources. The memo does not specify a mechanism for controlling those instructions.
sections.plainLanguage: Some SGML processors may run commands while reading a document. A recipient should account for that risk before processing untrusted SGML.
